P1.evidence: Second call in a sequence with a single purpose - hearing the partner's answer. The rep opened straight into it: 'we had a lovely conversation yesterday, so just curious, how did it go?' No frame is required or expected here.

P2.evidence: Baseline was taken in full on the previous day's call and none of it was repeated.

P3.evidence: Goals work belongs to the prior call. Worth noting for the coach that when the prospect said the price was too much, none of the previously established motivation - the heart attack and stroke fear, the Medicare clients on thirteen medications, saving his own life - was brought back to weigh against it.

P5.evidence: Belongs to the prior call. The script does say that hesitation returns you to Phase 5, and an explicit 'it's just going to have to be a no' is more than hesitation - but on a ten-minute follow-up with a real budget ceiling, rebuilding the consequence frame was a legitimate call to skip.

P6.evidence: Commitment was established and confirmed on the prior call, and the prospect restated it here unprompted: 'I literally want to do it so bad, but it's just the money.'

P11.evidence: A close was attempted on the downsell and none of the phase ran. No payment was taken and no link was actually sent - 'I'll just send a link for that' was followed by the decision being parked until Friday. No agreement, no community access, no onboarding form. The Trevor onboarding step does not apply to the group product. Defensible given the partner has to agree, but the prospect said 'I think it's doable' and nothing was attempted on that.

objection_plays.detail: The full financial picture had been taken the day before, so re-running it was unnecessary. What ran here was the reframe - 'we never want to let that be the reason that we can make something happen' - followed by cash on hand and a step-up test: told $175 was the maximum, the rep asked 'Do you think you can push that to 200?' of a man with a 620 credit score and near-maxed cards. The scripted move at this point is to make it work at the price, not to lower the price; instead the rep changed the product.

The partner objection is now the operative one - 'we've promised each other we're not going to make these decisions without each other.' None of the scripted moves ran: no 'money aside, do you personally feel this can get you there', no 'what obstacles might come up', no 'is there any reason he would NOT want you healthier', no permission-versus-input reframe. What the rep did instead was better than average practice - he asked whether Josh could join immediately, then booked a joint call at Josh's own preferred hour and asked for his name so he could address him directly on Friday.

There is no play in the process for what happened here, which is a downsell. A prospect said no to the flagship on price and was moved to a cheaper group product inside ninety seconds, at a price the playbook does not contain, with an improvised credit-toward-the-flagship promise attached. Whether that is the right commercial move is a management question, but the process has nothing to say about when it is permitted, at what price, or on what terms - which is why the same product has now been quoted four different ways in eight days.

notes: A well-judged ten minutes on the human side - he did not argue with the no, he kept the relationship, and he booked the partner onto the next call at the partner's own hour, which is the single best OB substitute in this batch. The problems are all structural rather than behavioural: an undocumented downsell at an undocumented price, a credit-toward-the-one-to-one promise made on the spot, a refundable deposit quietly redirected into a different purchase, and an ask to stretch a stated maximum on a prospect whose finances were disclosed as distressed the day before.
